title: Closest Pair of Keys in a Search Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary search tree with at least two nodes and all values distinct. Return the smallest difference between the values of any two nodes in the tree, not only a parent and its child.

examples.why: 48 is the right child of 20, but its closest value is the root 50. Sorted, the values are 20, 48, 50, 70.
Sorted: 27, 34, 44, 50, 58. The gaps are 7, 10, 6, 8, so the answer is the gap between 44 and 50.

constraints: The input is a valid binary search tree
hints: If the values were in a sorted list, which pairs would you need to compare?
In sorted order, the closest pair is always two neighbours. An in-order walk of a search tree visits the values in sorted order.
Do an in-order traversal, remember the previous value you visited, and track the smallest current − previous.

explain.intuition:
In a sorted list, the two closest values are always next to each other: anything between them would be closer to both. So you never need all pairs, only adjacent ones in sorted order.

A binary search tree already gives you sorted order for free: an in-order walk (left, node, right) visits the values from smallest to largest. Keep the previous value you visited and compare it with the current one. This catches pairs like 48 and 50 in the first example, which are far apart in the tree but neighbours in sorted order.
steps: Walk the tree in order, using a stack: go left as far as possible, then visit the node, then go to its right subtree.
When visiting a node, if prev is set, update best with node.val − prev. Then set prev = node.val.
pitfalls: Comparing only parents with their children. The closest value to a node is often its in-order neighbour higher up, like the root.
Initialising prev to 0. The first comparison then uses a value that is not in the tree. Use null or a sentinel that cannot win.
Sorting the values when the tree already gives them in order. That works, but wastes the search tree property.

complexity.space: O(h) for the stack, where h is the tree height

solutions.title: Collect and sort
solutions.idea: Gather every value with any traversal, sort them and take the smallest adjacent gap.

solutions.title: In-order walk with the previous value
solutions.idea: In-order visits values in sorted order, so compare each value only with the one visited just before it.

followups: The tree is an ordinary binary tree, not a search tree. What does the answer cost now?
Values arrive one at a time and you must report the smallest gap after each insert. Which structure keeps that cheap?
